newsitem.title: INDIA: FOCUS-India RBI credit policy ease sparks rate cut.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-India RBI credit policy ease sparks rate cut.

text.p: India's central bank on Saturday announced a more relaxed credit policy for the final six months of the 1996/97 budget year (April-March) and immediately prompted one bank to cut interest rates.

Reserve Bank of India governor Chakravarty Rangarajan outlined the bank's monetary policy to a news conference and said he expected a revival in the country's flagging industrial production growth rate.

The RBI's strategy received a warm welcome from bankers, industry and analysts looking for some comfort after the dismal performance of the country's markets during the past few weeks. "I think overall the policy is positive and should improve market sentiments. It is an attempt to kickstart the economy," S.R. Krishnan, banking analyst at Peregrine India said.

"In the second half industrial production will pick up," the RBI's Rangarajan said. "While the industrial growth will be lower than what it was in the previous year, it could nevertheless be expected to be around nine to 10.0 percent."
Industrial production data for the first quarter (April-June) showed growth of 8.5 percent, against 14.7 percent in the corresponding quarter a year ago.
The RBI moves to inject more liquidity into the banking system included cutting banks' cash reserve ratio requirements to 10 percent from 12 in four stages between now and end-January.
Each percentage point cut will increase banks' lending resources by 42.75 billion rupees, the RBI said.

That exceeded most expectations and the analysts welcomed the RBI's caution in saying that the final two 0.5 percentage point cuts planned for January would depend upon prevailing monetary and price conditions.
The central bank also lowered the cap on banks' interest rates on deposit accounts up to one year from 11 percent to 10.
The Bank of Baroda, one of the biggest state-run banks, immediately announced a cut in its prime lending rate to 15.0 percent from 15.5 percent, effective Monday.
And a senior Corporation Bank official told Reuters his bank is planning to cut its prime rate to 14.5 percent from 15.5, but was waiting for board approval.
The RBI governor said he expected banks to respond by immediately cutting rates by one percentage point at least.
Before the RBI policy announcement, banks' prime rates had ranged between 15.5 and 19.0 percent.

"This is a good policy. It meets the expectations of a wide cross-section.... industry, exporters, stock market. A good deal of operational freedom is also being given to banks to determine their own interest rates and spreads over prime rates," K.Kannan, chairman of the Bank of Baroda, told Reuters.

Among other measures announced, the RBI said it will allow banks to lend funds from expatriate Indians' foreign currency accounts to domestic borrowers, provided the loans were for productive investment.

The central bank also said banks can now buy shares and bonds in the secondary market provided the investment was limited to 5.0 percent of the additional deposits that banks mobilise in the current year over the previous year.
The RBI in order to promote exports also raised banks' export credit target to 12 percent from 10 percent, and the banks must attain these levels by the end of March.

"The CRR cut will definitely inject liquidity into the market but more importantly for stock markets, allowing banks to invest in secondary market will psychologically give a good boost," Hemendra Kothari, chairman of DSP Financial Consultants said, Indian affiliate of Merrill Lynch.
